source_text: τούτῳ φθειρομένης, ὡς ἀπολλύειν οἷον ἐκ τούτου τὸ καλεῖσθαι αἰώνιος τὸ γὰρ ὁτιδήποτε ἐξερχόμενον ἑαυτοῦ, τουτέστιν ἀλλασσόμενον, θάνατον εὑρίσκει, κἂν ἄλλως διαμένει, τὴν ἰδίαν ἀλλοίωσιν. καὶ γὰρ ὅπερ ἂν νοήσαις γεγενῆσθαι ἔπειτα, τοῦτο θάνατος τοῦ προτέρου ἐστίν· οἷόν τι ἡ κακία γενομένη ἀγαθότης θανατοῦται αὐτῷ, ᾧ ἀπέστη, ὑπὸ τῆς ἀγαθότητος· καὶ τὸ ἔμπαλιν, ἡ ἀγαθότης ὑπὸ τῆς κακίας. ἔστιν γάρ τινα, ἅπερ ἀεὶ ἑστάναι τῷ πρώτῳ ὅρῳ, εἰ καὶ μὴ ἠρνήθη τοῦτο αὐτοῖς, οὐκ ἀνέχεται. τοιγαροῦν διαγορεύουσιν ἐν ἐπιστολαῖς ταῦτα, Πέτρος μέν· «εἰ γὰρ ἀγγέλων ἁμαρτησάντων οὐκ ἐφείσατο ὁ θεός. ἀλλὰ σειραῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας, εἰς κρίσιν μεγάλης ἡμέρας τετήρηκεν καὶ ἀρ χαίου κόσμου οὐκ ἐφείσατο·» Ἰούδας δέ· 56 «ἀγγέλους τὲ τοὺς μὴ τηρήσαντες τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχήν, ἀλλ' ἀπολι πόντας τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον, δεσμοῖς ἀιδίοις εἰς κρίσιν μεγάλας ἡμέρας ὑπὸ ζόφον τετήρηκεν.» ἡ δὲ σωματικὴ λογικὴ κτίσις ἀλλοίωσιν δέχεται· κατὰ ἕξιν μὲν ὡς ὁ Ἰούδας τὸν ἁγιασμὸν ἀπολέσας· καὶ ὡς Παῦλος γράφει· «ἡ δὲ σπαταλῶσα χήρα, ζῶσα τέθνηκεν·» καίτοι βίον ἀνύουσα τὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἔτι· κατ' οὐσίαν δέ, ὡς ἀπολήγουσα μὲν πρῶτον, ἔπειτα δὲ μεταπίπτουσα εἰς ἀθανασίαν. «δεῖ γάρ «φησίν,» τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσασθαι ἀφθαρσίαν, καὶ τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσασθαι ἀθανασίαν.» ἡ δὲ μὴ λογικὴ κτίσις τροπὴν ὑπομένει καὶ ἀπογίνεται· ὡς ἡνίκα τοῦ φωτὸς εἰς σκότος καὶ τοῦ ὕδατος εἰς αἷμα μεταπίπτοντος, προεφητεύετο· «αὕτη ἡ ἀλλοίωσις τῆς δεξιᾶς τοῦ ὑψίστου·» καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ· «ὁ οὐρανός,» φησίν, «καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσεται.» προεφητεύθη γάρ, ὡς ἔσονται καινοὶ οὐρανοὶ καὶ καινὴ γῆ. καὶ γὰρ ἀληθῆ πᾶν τὸ δεξάμενον ἀρχήν, ἔχει καὶ τέλος. τὸ δὲ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ἅτε τῆς ἀρρήτου καὶ πάντων ἐπικρατούσης αἰωνίου καὶ ἀφθάρτου φύσεως ὑπάρχον, καὶ ἀεὶ ὡσαύτως καὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ ἔχον· μόνον τε εἰδὸς καὶ ποιοῦν τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ· καὶ φρουρητικὸν πάντων ὂν τῶν τε λογικῶν καὶ τὴν πίστιν τελείων, τῶν τε μὴ λογικῶν, ἕως τοῦ δοθέντος τοῖς μὴ λογικοῖς ὅρου τῆς ἐν ταυτότητι διαμονῆς· φύσει καὶ προαιρέσει τροπῆς καὶ μεταβολῆς ἀνεπίδεκτον καθέστηκεν, ὅ ἐστιν ἄφθαρτον. τὸ δὲ ἄτρεπτον ἤγουν ἄφθαρτον, εὐθὺς ἄναρχον, ἀτελεύτητον καὶ ὑπεραιώνιόν ἐστιν. τὸ δὲ ἄναρχον· δημιουργὸς καὶ οὐ δημιούργημα. διὸ κυρίως λέγει ἡ μὲν Σοφία· «τὸ ἄφθαρτόν σου πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἐν πᾶσιν·» ὁ δὲ Πέτρος· «ἐν τῷ ἀφθάρτῳ τοῦ πραέως καὶ ἡσυχίου πνεύματος.» οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἴσος αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ καὶ ὅμοιος ἀεὶ ὑπάρχων, μήτ' ἔνδοσιν πρὸς τὸ χεῖρον, μήτ' ἐπίτασιν πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον δεχόμενος, ἤκουσεν ὑπὸ Ἰακώβου· «παρ' ᾧ οὐκ ἔνι παραλλαγὴ ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα·» καὶ παρὰ Παύλου· «ἀφθάρτῳ, ἀοράτῳ, μόνῳ σοφῷ θεῷ·» ὃν τρόπον καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ἐν ραʹ Ψαλμῷ ἐμαρτυρήθη· «σὺ δέ, κύριε, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα μένεις,» καὶ πάλιν· «κατ' ἀρχὰς τὴν γῆν σύ, κύριε, ἐθεμελίωσας, καὶ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σού εἰσιν οἱ οὐρανοί. αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμένεις· καὶ πάντες ὡς ἱμάτιον παλαιωθήσονται· καὶ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον εἱλίξεις αὐτοὺς καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται· σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς ἀεὶ καὶ τὰ ἔτη σου οὐκ ἐκλείψουσιν.» 6.4ν ὅτι αἰώνιον ἡ κτίσις οὐ καθάπαξ καὶ αὐτοτελῶς τὸ αἰώνιον κέκτηται, πρῶτον μὲν ἐπειδὴ οἴκοθεν τοῦτο οὐκ ἔχει, ἀλλ' ἔτυχεν αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ ἑξῆς, ἀφ' οὗ ἐγένετο, μεταδόσει τοῦ μόνως καὶ ὑπεραιωνίως ὄντος αὐτομάτου θεοῦ· ἀγαθὸς γὰρ ὢν οὗτος δημιουργεῖ καὶ τέλος· προιστάμενος τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ποιήσεως, φιλοτιμεῖται αὐτῇ αἰωνιότητα· δεύτερον δὲ διὰ τὰς ἐξηγηθείσας αἰτίας ἐν τῷ κεφαλαίῳ τῷ πρὸ τοῦδε. τὸ δὲ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ὡς φύσει τὸ αἰώνιον ἔχον, καθὰ προσῆκεν ἔχειν δημιουργὸν καὶ ἀγαθὸν πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ πάντα ἐνεργοῦν αἰωνίως καὶ οὔποτε μὲν αὐτὸ περατούμενον, τῶν δ' ὑπ' αὐτοῦ γενομένων δυνάμενον εἶναι περατωτικόν, ταύτῃ ἀνευφημήθη τῇ προσρήσει. μάθοιτε δὲ ἄν, εἴ μοι ἐπίσποισθε, τῇδε· Παῦλος Ἑβραίοις ἐπιστέλλει οὕτως· «ὃς διὰ πνεύματος αἰωνίου ἑαυτὸν ἄμωμον προσήνεγκεν τῷ θεῷ.» λέγει δὲ τὸν δεσπότην Χριστόν, τὸν ἐν τῇ σεπτῇ ἐνανθρωπήσει αὐτοῦ ἑαυτὸν διὰ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ἀνθ' ἡμῶν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ πατρὶ προσενηνοχότα. καὶ Πέτρος δὲ προσηχεῖ ἀκόλουθα, ὡς ἤδη ἐμνημονεύθη· «τὸ δὲ ῥῆμα τοῦ θεοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.» ῥῆμα γὰρ θεοῦ ἐνταῦθα καλεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ. διὰ γοῦν τῆς θεότητος τὴν ταυτότητα μνημονεύων τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ ὁ Παῦλος, τῇ αὐτῇ κέχρηται τοῦ ῥήματος εὐφημίᾳ· «ὁ θεός,» φησίν, «καὶ πατὴρ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ οἶδεν, ὁ ὢν εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας·» καὶ pass_a_gloss: [...] by this very thing being corrupted, so as to lose, as it were, out of this the being called eternal. For anything whatever going out of itself, that is, being altered, finds death, even if otherwise it remains: its own alteration. For whatever you may conceive to have come into being afterwards, this is the death of the former: as, for instance, wickedness having become goodness is put to death in him from whom it departed, by the goodness; and the reverse, goodness by wickedness. For there are some things which do not endure always to stand in the first boundary, even if this was not denied to them. Accordingly they declare these things in letters, Peter on the one hand: 'for if God did not spare angels who sinned, but, casting them into Tartarus with chains of gloom, has kept them for the judgment of the great day, and did not spare the ancient world'; and Jude (printed page 56 here): 'and angels who did not keep their own rule, but left behind their own dwelling, he has kept under gloom in everlasting bonds for the judgment of the great day.' And the bodily rational creation receives alteration: on the one hand according to disposition, as Judas having lost his sanctification; and as Paul writes: 'but the widow who lives in luxury, living, has died', although she is still completing the life among men; and on the other hand according to substance, as first ceasing, and then falling over into immortality. 'For it is necessary', he says, 'that this corruptible put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality.' And the non-rational creation undergoes turning and passes away: as when, the light falling over into darkness and the water into blood, it was being prophesied: 'this is the alteration of the right hand of the Most High'; and elsewhere: 'heaven', he says, 'and earth will pass by'. For it was prophesied that there will be new heavens and a new earth. For indeed true: everything that received a beginning also has an end. But the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as he is of the unspeakable and all-prevailing eternal and incorruptible nature, and always holding in the same way and according to the same things; and alone knowing and doing the things of God; and being guardian of all things, both of the rational ones and those perfect in faith, and of the non-rational ones, until the boundary given to the non-rational of their continuance in sameness: by nature and by choice he has stood not admitting of turning and change, which is incorruptible. And what is unturning, that is incorruptible, is straightway without beginning, without end and above the ages. And what is without beginning: maker and not thing made. Therefore Wisdom on the one hand says properly: 'your incorruptible Spirit is in all things'; and Peter on the other: 'in the incorruptible of the meek and quiet spirit.' For so also the Father, being himself always equal to himself and like, receiving neither slackening toward the worse nor tightening toward the better, heard from James: 'beside whom there is no variation or shadow of turning'; and from Paul: 'to the incorruptible, invisible, only wise God'; in which manner also the Son was witnessed to in the 101st psalm (English 102): 'but you, Lord, remain for the age', and again: 'at the beginnings you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are works of your hands. They will perish, but you continue; and all will grow old like a garment; and like a wrap you will roll them up and they will be changed; but you are the same always and your years will not fail.' 6.4ν [Chapter title:] That he is eternal. The creation does not possess the eternal once for all and complete in itself: first because it does not have this from home, but obtained it for what follows, from when it came to be, by the sharing out of the God who is alone and above the ages self-existent; for this one being good creates, and finally, presiding over his own making, he lavishes eternity on it; and second because of the causes set out in the chapter before this one. But the Holy Spirit, as having the eternal by nature, as it befitted the creating and good Spirit of God to have, working all things eternally and never itself being bounded, but able to be a bounder of the things that came to be by it, was acclaimed with this title. You would learn, if you follow me, in this way: Paul writes to Hebrews thus: 'who through eternal Spirit offered himself blameless to God.' And he speaks of the Master Christ, who in his reverend becoming man offered himself through the Holy Spirit in our stead to his own Father. And Peter too sounds in agreement, as was already recalled: 'but the word of God remains for the age.' For here he calls the Spirit of God word of God. pass_b_english: … thing it is corrupted, so that on this account it loses, as it were, its title to be called eternal. For anything whatever that goes out of itself, that is, is altered, meets death, even if it lasts on in some other way: its own alteration is that death. Whatever you may conceive as having come to be afterwards is the death of what was there before. So, for instance, when wickedness turns into goodness, it is put to death by the goodness in the one from whom it has departed; and conversely, goodness is put to death by wickedness. For there are some beings that will not bear to stand always in their first station, although this was never denied them.

So it is that Peter and Jude state this plainly in their letters. Peter: “For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them into Tartarus in chains of gloom and has kept them for the judgment of the great day, and did not spare the ancient world …” (2 Peter 2:4-5). And Jude: “And the angels who did not keep their own original rank, but abandoned their proper dwelling, he has kept under gloom in everlasting bonds for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6).

The bodily rational creation admits alteration. It is altered in disposition, as when Judas lost his sanctification, and as Paul writes: “But the widow who lives for pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:6), though she is still living out her life among men. And it is altered in substance, when it first comes to an end and then passes over into immortality. “For this corruptible,” he says, “must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53).

The non-rational creation undergoes turning and passes away. So, when the light was turning into darkness and the water into blood, it was prophesied: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” And elsewhere: “Heaven,” he says, “and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35). For it was prophesied that there will be new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). And this is true: everything that has received a beginning also has an end.

But the Holy Spirit is of the ineffable nature that rules over all things, eternal and incorruptible. He is always the same and in the same respects. He alone knows and does the things of God (1 Corinthians 2:11). He guards all things: the rational beings who are perfect in faith, and the non-rational too, until the term given to the non-rational for their continuance in sameness. So by nature and by will he stands incapable of turning and change; that is, he is incorruptible. What cannot turn, that is, what is incorruptible, is at once without beginning, without end and above the ages; and what is without beginning is the Maker, not a thing made. That is why Wisdom says with full propriety: “Your incorruptible Spirit is in all things” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:1); and Peter: “in the incorruptibility of the gentle and quiet spirit” (1 Peter 3:4).

So too the Father, who is always equal to himself and like himself, admitting neither slackening toward the worse nor heightening toward the better, is spoken of by James as the one “with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning” (James 1:17), and by Paul as “the incorruptible, invisible, only wise God” (1 Timothy 1:17). In the same way the Son too was attested in the hundred and second Psalm: “But you, Lord, remain for ever” (Psalm 102:12); and again: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed; but you are the same always, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 102:25-27; Hebrews 1:10-12).

Creation does not possess eternity once for all and in its own right. First, because it does not have it of itself: it obtained it for the time to come, from the moment it came to be, as a gift shared by the God who alone, and above the ages, exists of himself. For being good he creates, and in the end, presiding over his own work, he generously bestows eternity on it. Secondly, for the reasons explained in the chapter before this one.

But the Holy Spirit has eternity by nature, as befitted the creating and good Spirit of God, who works all things eternally, is never himself bounded, and yet can set bounds to the things made by him; and so he was honoured with this title. You may learn this, if you will follow me, in the following way. Paul writes to the Hebrews: “who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God” (Hebrews 9:14). He means Christ the Master, who in his holy incarnation offered himself through the Holy Spirit to his own Father in our place. Peter too sounds the same note, as was already mentioned: “But the word of God remains for ever” (1 Peter 1:25). For here he calls the Spirit of God “word of God”. Indeed, because the Godhead of the Father and of the Son is the same, Paul, when he mentions them, uses the same reverent expression: “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “knows, he who is blessed for ever” (2 Corinthians 11:31); and again: “Jesus Christ yesterday and …

choices.issue: Old draft cut short, garbled, one name wrong
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English (about two thirds of the needed length) ended at 'And the one without beginning:' followed by a stray paragraph 'self-acting God', dropping the rest of chapter 6.3 (from δημιουργὸς καὶ οὐ δημιούργημα: Wisdom 12:1, 1 Peter 3:4, James 1:17, 1 Timothy 1:17, Psalm 102:12 and 102:25-27) and all of chapter 6.4 (creation's borrowed eternity, Hebrews 9:14, 1 Peter 1:25, 2 Corinthians 11:31, the start of Hebrews 13:8). It wrote 'Jude' for ὁ Ἰούδας who lost his sanctification (Judas), 'falling into immortality' for passing over into immortality, made the Spirit 'perfecting the faith of the irrational', and misread 'wickedness turned to goodness' and 'some beings will not bear to stand in their first station'. Bracket filler [it] removed. References added: 2 Peter 2:4-5 (old gave 2:4 and 2:5 apart), Isaiah 65:17, 1 Corinthians 2:11, and all those of the dropped text. The chapter title 6.4ν stands as its own paragraph.

choices.term: τούτῳ φθειρομένης
choices.english: … thing it is corrupted
choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence (the previous section ends καὶ αὐτῷ, 'and by this very'); only this section's words are translated, with a leading ellipsis.

choices.term: ἡ κακία γενομένη ἀγαθότης θανατοῦται αὐτῷ, ᾧ ἀπέστη, ὑπὸ τῆς ἀγαθότητος
choices.english: when wickedness turns into goodness, it is put to death by the goodness in the one from whom it has departed
choices.why: Read as 'wickedness, having become goodness, is put to death'; this gives the symmetry of the next clause (goodness by wickedness).

choices.term: ἑστάναι τῷ πρώτῳ ὅρῳ … οὐκ ἀνέχεται
choices.english: will not bear to stand always in their first station
choices.why: ὅρος here is the first bound or station given to a creature; it prepares for Jude's angels who 'did not keep their own original rank'.

choices.term: Ἰούδας δέ· 56 «…»
choices.english: And Jude:
choices.why: The letter-writer Jude. 56 is a printed page number in the copy-text; page debris, omitted.

choices.term: ὡς ὁ Ἰούδας τὸν ἁγιασμὸν ἀπολέσας
choices.english: as when Judas lost his sanctification
choices.why: With the article and as an example of a rational bodily creature altered in disposition, this is Judas Iscariot, not Jude the letter-writer (a reader report flagged the old 'Jude').

choices.term: τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχήν
choices.english: their own original rank
choices.why: ἀρχή in Jude 6 is both rule and beginning; 'original rank' keeps both and links to Didymus' 'first station'.

choices.term: κατὰ ἕξιν μέν … κατ' οὐσίαν δέ
choices.english: altered in disposition … altered in substance
choices.why: The μέν/δέ pair; ἕξις is moral state, οὐσία the being itself (death and resurrection).

choices.term: μεταπίπτουσα εἰς ἀθανασίαν
choices.english: passes over into immortality
choices.why: μεταπίπτω is to change over, not to fall; the old 'falling into immortality' was garbled.

choices.term: αὕτη ἡ ἀλλοίωσις τῆς δεξιᾶς τοῦ ὑψίστου
choices.english: This is the change of the right hand of the Most High
choices.why: Greek Psalm 76:11 (English 77:10), which differs from the Hebrew; no inline reference (see added_allusions).

choices.term: καὶ γὰρ ἀληθῆ
choices.english: And this is true
choices.why: Elliptic ('for indeed [these are] true'); rendered as a short affirmation.

choices.term: μόνον τε εἰδὸς καὶ ποιοῦν τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ
choices.english: He alone knows and does the things of God (1 Corinthians 2:11)
choices.why: Allusion to 1 Corinthians 2:11, where only the Spirit of God knows the things of God.

choices.term: τῶν τε λογικῶν καὶ τὴν πίστιν τελείων
choices.english: the rational beings who are perfect in faith
choices.why: The καί joins two descriptions of one group (rational and perfect in faith), set against the non-rational.

choices.term: ἕως τοῦ δοθέντος τοῖς μὴ λογικοῖς ὅρου τῆς ἐν ταυτότητι διαμονῆς
choices.english: until the term given to the non-rational for their continuance in sameness
choices.why: The non-rational creation is guarded only until the end set for it (it 'passes away'); kept literal.

choices.term: ἐν τῷ ἀφθάρτῳ τοῦ πραέως καὶ ἡσυχίου πνεύματος
choices.english: in the incorruptibility of the gentle and quiet spirit
choices.why: Didymus quotes only these words of 1 Peter 3:4; no noun such as 'ornament' is supplied.

choices.term: ἤκουσεν ὑπὸ Ἰακώβου
choices.english: is spoken of by James as
choices.why: Literally 'heard from James' (was so addressed); turned into a plain passive.

choices.term: ἐν ραʹ Ψαλμῷ
choices.english: the hundred and second Psalm
choices.why: Greek Psalm 101 is English Psalm 102. εἱλίξεις ('roll up') is the wording of Hebrews 1:12, so both are cited.

choices.term: μεταδόσει τοῦ μόνως καὶ ὑπεραιωνίως ὄντος αὐτομάτου θεοῦ
choices.english: as a gift shared by the God who alone, and above the ages, exists of himself
choices.why: αὐτόματος of God: existing of himself; the old stray 'self-acting God' came from this phrase.

choices.term: ταύτῃ ἀνευφημήθη τῇ προσρήσει
choices.english: and so he was honoured with this title
choices.why: The title is 'eternal' from the chapter heading (Hebrews 9:14 'eternal Spirit').

choices.term: τῇ αὐτῇ κέχρηται τοῦ ῥήματος εὐφημίᾳ
choices.english: uses the same reverent expression
choices.why: The expression is 'for ever' (εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας), used of the Father here and of the Son in Hebrews 13:8.

choices.term: Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς χθὲς καὶ
choices.english: “Jesus Christ yesterday and …
choices.why: The quotation runs on into the next section; only this section's words are translated, so the reference is given there.
